title: In 299,670 human de novo mutations, conserved non-coding bases mutate 3-10% less than low-score control bases, and their calibrated gnomAD deficit is 3-6%, against 25-48% at conserved coding bases
abstract: Human non-coding DNA bases that conservation scores call constrained get 3-10% fewer new germline mutations than the control bases they are usually compared with, and after this is taken into account only a small shortage of human variants (3-6%) remains at them, against 25-48% at conserved protein-coding bases. This matters because a shortage of variants in large human samples is a main type of evidence that non-coding DNA has a function, and part of it is a mutation-rate signal. We used 299,670 de novo mutations (new mutations in a child that are not in the parents) from four public studies of 4,874 children, after removal of duplicate children and of likely inherited calls. We compared bases with a high phyloP conservation score with control bases of the same three-base sequence, GC content and 1-Mb region, and did the same for gnomAD v4.1 variant density (76,215 genomes) in identical strata. At non-CpG sites, bases conserved only in primates had 0.929 (95% CI 0.904-0.954) times the de novo rate of the usual control bases (primate score below 1.0), and bases conserved in mammals had 0.898 (0.873-0.923); against controls without bases that changed in primates the ratios were 0.973 and 0.971. The lower rate explains about two-thirds of the usual gnomAD deficit, and 35-45% against the cleaner controls. After calibration in low score bins assumed to be free of selection, the deficit left for selection was 3.3% (1.0-5.3) and 4.5% (2.2-6.6) of variant density, and 33% (28-38) at mammal-conserved coding bases (positive control); results were similar for singletons, older alleles and the cleaner controls, and smaller (1-2%, intervals include 0) against controls with scores of 1.0-1.3. The four studies agreed for these tests but not in one low-score bin. The rate falls as the score rises, at C/G bases mainly up to a score of 1.0. This confirms with unselected mutations a hypothesis that Barroso and Ragsdale (2026) based on mutation-rate maps. The 233-primate score cannot reach 1.3 at any A or T base. Limitations: de novo counts are small for single element sets, so the test of the primate-constrained DHS cores of Kuderna et al. 2024 is inconclusive; the calibration exponent differs between frequency classes for reasons we did not establish.
